name: Dermamelan
lead: Dermamelan is a professional depigmenting (skin-lightening) treatment from Mesoestetic, Barcelona, marketed for melasma and other uneven pigmentation. People use it to fade dark patches and get a more even, brighter complexion [1].

It is described in the literature as a non-hydroquinone bleaching formulation, developed in a field where hydroquinone is the most popular depigmenting agent but treatment of melasma is described as unsatisfactory [1][2]. It is applied in a clinic setting and discussed in appearance communities as a way to even out skin tone.

A 2011 open-label pilot study of ten women with melasma, using reflectance confocal microscopy alongside standard scoring, reported about a 50% improvement in the Melasma Area and Severity Index with only mild irritation as an adverse event [1][3].
infobox: 10 women, Fitzpatrick types II-IV, 3 months of treatment [3]

paras: One pilot study, published in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology in 2011, enrolled ten women with melasma (Fitzpatrick skin types II to IV) in an open-label trial lasting four months, with Dermamelan applied once daily for three months. Assessments included the Melasma Area and Severity Index, standard and UV-light photographs and in vivo reflectance confocal microscopy [1][3].

Reported results: MASI improved by about 50%, with the greatest effect usually within one month and persisting one month after treatment ended. Microscopy showed a significant decrease in pigmented epidermal keratinocytes; patients with melanophages at baseline had poorer outcomes. Mild irritation was the only adverse event and most patients were satisfied. The authors concluded Dermamelan produced rapid improvement at clinical and cellular levels [3]. No other published trials were identified.

Melasma is a common pigmentary disorder caused by abnormal melanin deposits in the skin, and hydroquinone is the most popular depigmenting agent, although results are described as unsatisfactory [1]. Wikipedia describes melasma as chronic and relapsing, triggered by UV exposure, hormones (pregnancy, contraceptives) and genetics, and more common in women and people with darker skin [2].

Other options listed there include hydroquinone at 2% over the counter or 4% by prescription, oral tranexamic acid, chemical peels, azelaic acid, kojic acid and combination creams, with strict sun protection stressed; treatments can cause irritation, scarring, lighter patches and contact dermatitis [2].

card.summary: A professional non-hydroquinone depigmenting treatment for melasma, backed by one small pilot study.
card.note: Only a single 2011 pilot study was found; depigmenting treatments can cause irritation and should be professionally supervised according to dermatology guidance generally.

quick.overview:
Dermamelan is a depigmenting treatment marketed for melasma and uneven pigmentation. It is described in the literature as a non-hydroquinone bleaching formulation.

The published evidence is limited to one small pilot study from 2011 that used confocal microscopy to examine the skin.
quick.mechanism: It is intended to reduce melanin deposits in the skin; the available source describes it as an alternative to hydroquinone, the most widely used depigmenting agent.
quick.risks: Safety was assessed in the pilot study, but larger trials have not been identified, so the full adverse-effect profile is not documented in the sources reviewed.

chain: Depigmenting formulation is applied to areas of melasma
Melanin production and pigmented keratinocytes in the epidermis decrease
angle.text: Dermamelan is used to lighten melasma patches and hyperpigmentation for a more even complexion. In the pilot study, melasma scores improved by about half over a three-month treatment.
